title: The table of winners
intro: A multibagger table makes small-cap fortunes look routine. Before you believe it, open the study behind it.

facts.label: The table
facts.value: Rows of 100-baggers and 50-baggers, mostly small companies bought cheap at past market bottoms. The apparent ease is striking.

facts.label: The missing rows
facts.value: The table records the winners; the many small companies that simply failed are not in it.

facts.label: The four-bottoms study
facts.value: Hurdles for outlier status by 2026: 100× from 2009 (31%/yr), 50× from 2012–13 (32–35%/yr), 25× from 2016 (38%/yr), 10× from 2020 (47%/yr).

facts.label: The base rates
facts.value: From 2009, 2012, 2013 and 2016: roughly ONE IN TEN listed companies cleared the bar — a steady crop from ordinary corrections. From 2020: close to ONE IN THREE.

facts.label: The 2020 anomaly
facts.value: Shortest runway, steepest hurdle, highest hit rate — the difference was the distressed prices on offer at entry. The bounce alone packed years of return into quarters.

question: What's the honest reading of the winners table?
choices: Small caps reliably make fortunes — buy any basket and wait
Survivorship hides the failures, but bottoms genuinely mint outliers (~1 in 10; ~1 in 3 from 2020's panic prices) — the entry discount, not routine skill, did the heaviest lifting
Multibaggers are pure luck and the study means nothing
debrief: Two truths at once. The table IS survivorship-biased — its ease is illusory because the failed companies aren't in it. AND the four-bottoms study finds something real: ordinary corrections leave a consistent ~1-in-10 crop of eventual outliers, while 2020's panic pricing lifted the rate to ~1-in-3 despite the steepest hurdle — because buying sound assets at distressed prices packs years of return into the bounce. The synthesis: corrections are the opportunity, base rates are the humility, and the table's job is neither — it's marketing. Pre-decide what you'd buy at the next bottom; expect one-in-ten, not every-row.
